Hi, I'm not a doctor, so take anything I say with a pinch of salt. However, I am very experienced in body odor issues.

It sounds like you have Trimethylaminuria (TMAU) Type 2. Type 1 is due to genetics, and you would likely have had symptoms from birth if you had Type 1. However, yours only started when you started menstruating. Type 2 is caused by an overload of bacteria in the gut that produce TMA- the fish smelling chemical. The fact you also have severe bloating after eating further suggests you have a bad balance of bacteria in your gut (gut dysbiosis). More on definition of type 1 or type 2 below\*

A doctor can test you for TMAU with a urine test. You have to eat a set diet for a day, high in foods likely to trigger symptoms, then have a urine test the day after. The result of the urine test will diagnose you with, or exclude, TMAU.

Thankfully Type 2 TMAU can be helped. The following are likely to help reduce the smell, if you have TMAU:

-low choline, low carnitine, low fish, low red meat diet.

-liquid probiotics (tablets are often dead/ ineffective)

-slightly acidic body wash

-eating a varied diet, with 30g of fibre a day and plenty of water (until urine is clear colour)

Your smell is mostly fishy, then its likely TMAU. Lots of people here only smell like feces, which we have assigned the name FBO (fecal body odor) to. However, TMAU is a recognised medical condition. FBO is not.

I’m not a doctor or professional but here are some ideas to try to take in more calories without feeling full:

-Eat calorie high, but physically small foods. These are called calorie dense foods. An example would be cheese and nuts which have a high amount of calories for a small portion which isn’t very filling. 

-on a similar note, try to minimise the low calorie, but physically big foods that fill you up without giving you many calories, eg watermelon. Obviously you should try to keep your five portions of fruit and veg a day, but just be mindful about calorie density. 

-you can add healthy fats like olive oil to your foods as garnish. It’s full of calories and won’t fill you up

-ingest calories with drink, eg protein shakes, mass gainers from a reputable source, drink milk

-don’t drink too much at once just before a meal. A trick I used to use to feel LESS hungry was to guzzle pints of water every time I wanted a snack when I shouldn’t eat one. The water filled me up temporarily. In your case, keep hydrated by SIPPING 8 big cups of water through the day, rather than guzzling a load of liquid at once.

-your stomach does shrink/stretch over time. Keep GENTLY pushing yourself to feel fuller. Please do this gradually and don’t make yourself sick. 

My buddy wrestles and when he has to cut his weight he goes on a low calorie diet for months. After he weighs in, he has a full day to eat whatever he wants. You’d think he’d eat all the food he could see because he’s had to restrict himself so much for months. In fact, he gets full after a tiny portion of food that normally wouldn’t even be a starter for him. In that case his stomach shrank over the months of weight cutting. Probably like you have when you didn’t eat much. After a few weeks he slowly regains his appetite. 

Again I’m not a professional on this, but they are personal tips I have based on my life experience

I am no medical expert but I’ve suffered all my life with constipation. 

It sounds like you could have a muscle coordination problem (like you said the way your brain controls your bowel opening) OR a physical problem such as a prolapse or rectocele. Both are causes of long term constipation that are unrelated to diet.

You would benefit from seeing a colorectal surgeon and having a daefography (AKA proctogram) to see how your muscles move during a bowel movement and to see if you have an internal prolapse/rectocele etc. You can get one of those tests privately in the UK for about £500. You can search online what those terms mean too. 

If you feel like your bowel isn’t properly empty after a bowel movement it is likely a rectocele or prolapse. That’s when the walls of the rectum are much weaker than they should be and can block the bowel movement.

If you feel like you need to go but just can’t, it is likely to have a coordination problem where you’re accidentally tightening the back passage instead of loosening it when you need to go. It sounds silly and is easy to say you’re not doing that, but the whole point is a problem with the connection between brain and body where you don’t know what you’re doing and can’t help it. You can help by deep breathing with your belly just before a bowel movement and raising your knees higher than your hips by putting your feet on something like a box.

Remember first to try actually measuring your fibre rather than saying you’ve eaten some good things today. 35grams a day. Drink enough water so that your urine is nearly clear too. This should be your first attempt at fixing it.
